messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 58
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Fisherman
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 65

He is 58, a South Asian fisherman who has spent most of his life reading water the way other men read faces. Before the accident, he works long hours without complaint, leaving before dawn, gutting and sorting the catch by instinct, and returning home with the smell of salt and diesel in his clothes. His wife used to tease him that even in sleep he listens for the tide. Since her death some years earlier, he lives alone, keeping to routines that make the days feel manageable. The sea remains the one place where he feels he knows himself.

The accident happens on an ordinary morning, which is part of what stays with him. The weather is not especially bad. He remembers the sky being pale and the water choppy but familiar, nothing he has not handled many times before. He is out with two younger men when a mechanical failure jams the winch as they are hauling gear. In the confusion, a line whips loose and catches him hard. He loses his footing and is thrown against the side of the boat before going over. He remembers the shock of cold more than pain at first, the water slamming into his chest and stealing his breath. Then there is the soundless panic of being dragged by the tangled line, the boat still moving, salt filling his mouth, his body no longer his own.

He tells the story in fragments because that is how it comes to him. He remembers seeing the prop wash above him like white smoke. He remembers thinking, very clearly, so this is how I die. He thinks of his wife in that instant, not in any grand or peaceful way, but with a sharp, guilty flash: that he will leave no one to close up the house properly, no one to know what to do with his things. One of the younger men cuts the line and they haul him back aboard. By then he is vomiting seawater, shaking uncontrollably, unable to speak. He survives with bruised ribs, deep rope burns, and a shoulder injury that heals more quickly than the fear.

In the first weeks afterward, everyone tells him he is lucky. He nods because he knows this is true. He also knows something in him has changed. He tries to return to work before he is ready. The first time he steps back onto a boat, his legs stiffen. He tells himself not to be foolish, but his heart starts pounding so hard he feels it in his throat. Every creak of metal sounds like a warning. When someone drops a coil of rope near him, he flinches so violently the younger crewmen stare. He laughs it off, ashamed.

At night he sleeps lightly, if at all. He wakes drenched, convinced for a few seconds that he is underwater. In the dreams there is no rescue. Sometimes he is tangled and sinking; sometimes he surfaces beside the boat and no one sees him. He starts avoiding sleep because he does not want to go back there. He dozes in a chair with the television on, then wakes abruptly, disoriented and angry with himself. During the day he is exhausted, but still restless. He checks weather reports obsessively, though he is no longer going out regularly. He sits at the harbor and studies the movement of other boats, scanning for danger as if vigilance alone could prevent disaster.

His world grows smaller in ways he does not immediately admit. He begins refusing jobs that would take him offshore. Then he stops going down to the docks unless necessary. Friends from the fishing community invite him for tea, but he often declines. He says he is tired or has paperwork to do. The truth is that hearing men talk casually about rough water, gear failures, and close calls makes his stomach clench. He feels set apart from them, weak in a way he has never allowed himself to be. He has spent a lifetime in an occupation that prizes steadiness, and now he cannot trust his own body not to betray him.

He is also troubled by how quickly irritation rises in him. Small things provoke outsized anger: a neighbor’s radio, a door slamming, the shriek of brakes in the street. He startles at the hiss of pressure cookers and the snap of clotheslines. Once, at the fish market, a crate topples behind him and he drops to a crouch before he understands where he is. He feels humiliated afterward and leaves without finishing his errands. More and more, he keeps to himself.

When he speaks about the accident now, he does so with long pauses, his gaze fixed somewhere beyond the room. He says the sea used to feel like home, even after his wife died. Now it feels like something waiting. He misses the work, the rhythm of it, the identity it gave him. Some mornings he stands at the shore before sunrise, hands in his pockets, breathing the briny air that once settled him. He wants to believe he can return to the life he knew. Instead he finds himself listening for the slap of water against wood, watching the ropes, calculating exits, his body already braced for disaster.
